content.text: All four failing sheets have had their briefs repaired and the specification text is back in sync.

input.summary: Repaired all four failing sheets in the figure briefs, with no change to the claims, the numeral table, or any disclosed embodiment. FIG. 1: the hidden broken-line chamber outline and the schematic fluid-communication line were the cause of both rejected endpoints, so the sheet is now an all-solid-line external perspective, the two housings are identified as left-hand (vibration motor 18) and right-hand (air-extraction mechanism 20) with plain front faces no line crosses, and the handle 44 is drawn as a closed outline enclosing an open area so its leader has an interior region to terminate in. The chamber 22 keeps its numeral and its definition and is shown on FIG. 2, the sectional view, where it is the broad white space between the legs. FIG. 3: the brief now requires exactly two rectangular outlines and states that the base edge and the outer edge of the perimeter member 24 are one and the same line, with no separate base outline, no third rectangle, and no frame. FIG. 4: numeral 26 is now targeted on the single lowest line of the column and expressly not in the hatching above or the open space below, and clearance 34 is targeted well inside the open space touching neither line, which separates the two adjacent targets. FIG. 5: numeral 10 moved from the outer silhouette to a broad interior target on the visible top face of the machine's base, the pulling element 46 now runs to the left with its target where it crosses the tile clear of the sheet edges, the tile 36 is targeted on the right of the machine away from the cord, and 24 is targeted clear of the corners where the band turns. Synchronized draft/06-drawings.md (FIG. 1 sentence) and one sentence of draft/07-detailed-description.md so that no application text claims a broken line or a chamber is visible in FIG. 1. All five briefs are now at or below 2800 characters, every sheet carries at most eight numerals, and the union of the five sheets is still exactly the 16-entry numeral table.
reasoning: Two of the three FIG. 1 rejections shared one cause: a hidden chamber outline in broken line plus a second broken line for the fluid communication, both squeezed under a slab in a perspective view. Numeral 20 kept landing on a dashed line instead of the pump housing, and numeral 22 kept landing on the chamber outline instead of inside it, because a hidden outline under a shallow band has almost no interior to aim at. Rather than keep retrying a target the geometry cannot support, I took the hidden work off FIG. 1 and let the section view carry the chamber. That is what FIG. 2 is for, and its 22 target, the broad white space between the legs, has never failed.

Moving the chamber cost the application nothing: numeral 22 keeps its single definition in draft/numerals.md, keeps every use in the description and claims, and still appears on a sheet. Nothing disclosed was deleted to satisfy a coverage rule. I did remove the canonical part name and numeral from the FIG. 1 brief entirely, as required when a numeral moves off a sheet, and the perimeter member bullet now describes the base standing clear of the tile without naming the chamber.

Because the FIG. 1 brief no longer draws those broken lines, two sentences of application text had become false. The Brief Description of the Drawings said the chamber was indicated in broken line and the fluid communication shown by a separate broken line, and the Detailed Description said the same. I corrected both to match: the FIG. 1 sentence now claims only the schematic handle, motor and air-extraction mechanism, and the Detailed Description says that no particular route for the fluid communication is shown in the drawings. The substantive relationship, that the air-extraction mechanism 20 is in fluid communication with the chamber 22, is untouched in the description and in claims 1, 10 and 14; only the assertion about what a sheet depicts changed.

The FIG. 1 housings were previously described as 'one of the two bodies' and 'the other body', which gives a renderer no way to tell 18 from 20 and gives a reviewer no way to check. They are now the left-hand and the right-hand housing, which is the stable naming the endpoint rule asks for, and each front face is declared a plain closed surface that no other line crosses so the endpoint cannot be read as sitting on a passing line.

Numeral 44's leader did not end in a dot because a grip drawn as a bare stroke has no interior. The handle is now drawn as one closed outline enclosing a visible open area, which is the simplest generic outline that gives the annotator somewhere to put a terminal dot. That is a depiction convention only; the brief still says no particular handle form is shown, and no handle shape, size, or mounting has been added to the description or the claims.

FIG. 3's three-rectangle artifact came from the renderer drawing the base underside as its own outline in addition to the two edges of the loop. The brief now states that the base edge and the outer edge of the perimeter member 24 are the same single line and that no separate outline is drawn for the base, and it forbids a third rectangle, a frame, and a border. The rectangular plan remains a declared depiction convention confined to this brief and is still absent from the application text.

FIG. 4's numeral 26 sits between two neighbours that are only a hair away: the hatching of the column above it and the clearance gap below it. Rather than an exact coordinate, I made the target self-disambiguating in words: the single lowest line of the column, on that line itself, neither in the hatching above nor in the open space below. Numeral 34 was tightened to match from the other side, well inside the open space and touching neither bounding line. The bearing face is a face seen edge on in a section, so a line target is the honest one; the fix is to make the line unmistakable rather than to invent a structure that would give it an interior.

FIG. 5 failed because 10 and 36 converged and because the cord had no stated direction, so the annotator could put the tile target and the device target in the same place and could run the cord under the numerals. Numeral 10 now has a broad interior target on the visible top face of the machine's base, which is unambiguous here because 12 is not on this sheet, and the cord now leaves to the left, which puts 36 on the open tile to the right and 46 on the cord where it crosses the tile clear of the sheet edges. Numeral 24 was landing on a corner vertex, so its target now says clear of the corners where the band turns.

Adding those clarifications pushed FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 over the 2800-character limit, so I bought the room back by cutting rendering constraints that do nothing: the column no longer has to stand in the right part of the sheet, and repeated boilerplate was compressed. No disclosed geometry, relationship, or numeral target was traded away to make room.

I changed nothing in the claims, the numeral table, the summary, or the abstract this turn. Every repair was to a figure brief, plus the two sentences of application text that described what a sheet shows and would otherwise have contradicted the repaired brief.
changes: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: removed the chamber 22 bullet, the hidden broken-line chamber outline, and the schematic fluid-communication line; declared every line solid with nothing hidden drawn; identified the vibration motor 18 as the left-hand housing and the air-extraction mechanism 20 as the right-hand housing, each with a plain closed front face no other line crosses; redrew the handle 44 as a closed outline enclosing a visible open area with the endpoint well inside that area; added 'clear of the corners where the band turns' to the perimeter member 24 target. Sheet numerals now 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44.

figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: required exactly two rectangular outlines with no third rectangle, frame or border, and stated that the edge of the base is the same single line as the outer edge of the perimeter member 24 so no separate base outline is drawn; added 'clear of the corners where the band turns' to the 24 target.

figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: bearing face 26 now targeted on the single lowest line closing the bottom of the column, anywhere along its length, neither in the hatching above it nor in the open space below it; clearance 34 targeted well inside the open unhatched space touching neither bounding line; exposed face 38 targeted on the tile top edge line and not in the space above it; removed the arbitrary constraint that the column stand in the right part of the sheet and compressed boilerplate to stay under 2800 characters.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: numeral 10 retargeted from the outer silhouette to the visible top face of the machine's base where no housing stands; flexible pulling element 46 now meets the machine on its left, runs left over the tile and leaves at the left edge, with its endpoint on the curved line over the tile clear of the machine and clear of the sheet edges; covering element 36 targeted on the exposed tile to the right of the machine, away from the cord; perimeter member 24 targeted clear of the corners where the band turns.

draft/06-drawings.md: the FIG. 1 sentence no longer states that the chamber is indicated in broken line or that the fluid communication is shown by a separate broken line; it now recites only the handle, vibration motor and air-extraction mechanism being shown schematically.

draft/07-detailed-description.md: 'The fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown.' replaced with 'No particular route is shown in the drawings for the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22.'
input.prior_art_strategy: Untouched by this turn, and deliberately so, since every repair was to drawing specifications. Claim 1 still rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously while extraction holds the chamber below atmospheric; on the all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and on the bearing face being slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained. Those clear DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, whose contacting walls are a rubber-elastic apron and elastic partitions that close the space, US-11408462-B2 using rigidity only as a frame restricting an elastic partition; US-10001245-B2, which holds in a vacuum suction mode and moves on a blower air cushion so the coupling is surrendered while it moves; US-11247858-B2, a perforated suction plate moved by an actuation system rather than slid while held; and US-4934475-A, whose vibration lifts the body to reduce the holding force so it walks along a wall. FIG. 4 remains the sheet that shows the clearance, which is the feature carrying the most weight against the sealing-cup art, and its repair strengthened rather than softened that depiction.
input.answer: All four failing sheets are repaired at the figure-brief level, and the application text now matches what those sheets actually show. FIG. 1 lost the hidden broken-line chamber and the schematic communication line that were pulling numerals 20 and 22 onto dashed strokes; it is now an all-solid-line external perspective with the motor and pump identified as the left-hand and right-hand housings, each with a plain front face, and with the handle drawn as a closed outline so numeral 44's leader has an interior to end in. The chamber keeps numeral 22, its definition, and every mention in the description and claims, and is shown on FIG. 2, the section view, where its target has always passed. FIG. 3 now requires exactly two rectangles and states that the base edge and the outer edge of the perimeter member are one line, which is what produced the spurious third rectangle. FIG. 4 separates the two adjacent targets in words: the bearing face is on the single lowest line of the column and expressly not in the hatching above or the gap below, and the clearance is well inside the gap touching neither line. FIG. 5 gives numeral 10 a broad interior target on the base top face instead of the silhouette it was sharing with the tile, sends the cord to the left so the tile target sits on the open right side, keeps the cord's own target over the tile and clear of the sheet edges, and moves the perimeter member target off the corner vertex. Two sentences of application text changed only because they described broken lines that no longer exist: the FIG. 1 entry in the Brief Description of the Drawings, and one sentence in the Detailed Description, which now says no particular route for the fluid communication is shown in the drawings. The fluid-communication relationship itself remains in the description and in claims 1, 10 and 14. Claims, numeral table, summary and abstract are unchanged; every brief is at or below 2800 characters, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, and the five sheets together still cover exactly the 16 numerals in the table. Whether the regenerated pixels now satisfy the OCR, semantic, leader and endpoint gates is for that pipeline to report on the next render.

structured_output.summary: Repaired all four failing sheets in the figure briefs, with no change to the claims, the numeral table, or any disclosed embodiment. FIG. 1: the hidden broken-line chamber outline and the schematic fluid-communication line were the cause of both rejected endpoints, so the sheet is now an all-solid-line external perspective, the two housings are identified as left-hand (vibration motor 18) and right-hand (air-extraction mechanism 20) with plain front faces no line crosses, and the handle 44 is drawn as a closed outline enclosing an open area so its leader has an interior region to terminate in. The chamber 22 keeps its numeral and its definition and is shown on FIG. 2, the sectional view, where it is the broad white space between the legs. FIG. 3: the brief now requires exactly two rectangular outlines and states that the base edge and the outer edge of the perimeter member 24 are one and the same line, with no separate base outline, no third rectangle, and no frame. FIG. 4: numeral 26 is now targeted on the single lowest line of the column and expressly not in the hatching above or the open space below, and clearance 34 is targeted well inside the open space touching neither line, which separates the two adjacent targets. FIG. 5: numeral 10 moved from the outer silhouette to a broad interior target on the visible top face of the machine's base, the pulling element 46 now runs to the left with its target where it crosses the tile clear of the sheet edges, the tile 36 is targeted on the right of the machine away from the cord, and 24 is targeted clear of the corners where the band turns. Synchronized draft/06-drawings.md (FIG. 1 sentence) and one sentence of draft/07-detailed-description.md so that no application text claims a broken line or a chamber is visible in FIG. 1. All five briefs are now at or below 2800 characters, every sheet carries at most eight numerals, and the union of the five sheets is still exactly the 16-entry numeral table.
reasoning: Two of the three FIG. 1 rejections shared one cause: a hidden chamber outline in broken line plus a second broken line for the fluid communication, both squeezed under a slab in a perspective view. Numeral 20 kept landing on a dashed line instead of the pump housing, and numeral 22 kept landing on the chamber outline instead of inside it, because a hidden outline under a shallow band has almost no interior to aim at. Rather than keep retrying a target the geometry cannot support, I took the hidden work off FIG. 1 and let the section view carry the chamber. That is what FIG. 2 is for, and its 22 target, the broad white space between the legs, has never failed.

Moving the chamber cost the application nothing: numeral 22 keeps its single definition in draft/numerals.md, keeps every use in the description and claims, and still appears on a sheet. Nothing disclosed was deleted to satisfy a coverage rule. I did remove the canonical part name and numeral from the FIG. 1 brief entirely, as required when a numeral moves off a sheet, and the perimeter member bullet now describes the base standing clear of the tile without naming the chamber.

Because the FIG. 1 brief no longer draws those broken lines, two sentences of application text had become false. The Brief Description of the Drawings said the chamber was indicated in broken line and the fluid communication shown by a separate broken line, and the Detailed Description said the same. I corrected both to match: the FIG. 1 sentence now claims only the schematic handle, motor and air-extraction mechanism, and the Detailed Description says that no particular route for the fluid communication is shown in the drawings. The substantive relationship, that the air-extraction mechanism 20 is in fluid communication with the chamber 22, is untouched in the description and in claims 1, 10 and 14; only the assertion about what a sheet depicts changed.

The FIG. 1 housings were previously described as 'one of the two bodies' and 'the other body', which gives a renderer no way to tell 18 from 20 and gives a reviewer no way to check. They are now the left-hand and the right-hand housing, which is the stable naming the endpoint rule asks for, and each front face is declared a plain closed surface that no other line crosses so the endpoint cannot be read as sitting on a passing line.

Numeral 44's leader did not end in a dot because a grip drawn as a bare stroke has no interior. The handle is now drawn as one closed outline enclosing a visible open area, which is the simplest generic outline that gives the annotator somewhere to put a terminal dot. That is a depiction convention only; the brief still says no particular handle form is shown, and no handle shape, size, or mounting has been added to the description or the claims.

FIG. 3's three-rectangle artifact came from the renderer drawing the base underside as its own outline in addition to the two edges of the loop. The brief now states that the base edge and the outer edge of the perimeter member 24 are the same single line and that no separate outline is drawn for the base, and it forbids a third rectangle, a frame, and a border. The rectangular plan remains a declared depiction convention confined to this brief and is still absent from the application text.

FIG. 4's numeral 26 sits between two neighbours that are only a hair away: the hatching of the column above it and the clearance gap below it. Rather than an exact coordinate, I made the target self-disambiguating in words: the single lowest line of the column, on that line itself, neither in the hatching above nor in the open space below. Numeral 34 was tightened to match from the other side, well inside the open space and touching neither bounding line. The bearing face is a face seen edge on in a section, so a line target is the honest one; the fix is to make the line unmistakable rather than to invent a structure that would give it an interior.

FIG. 5 failed because 10 and 36 converged and because the cord had no stated direction, so the annotator could put the tile target and the device target in the same place and could run the cord under the numerals. Numeral 10 now has a broad interior target on the visible top face of the machine's base, which is unambiguous here because 12 is not on this sheet, and the cord now leaves to the left, which puts 36 on the open tile to the right and 46 on the cord where it crosses the tile clear of the sheet edges. Numeral 24 was landing on a corner vertex, so its target now says clear of the corners where the band turns.

Adding those clarifications pushed FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 over the 2800-character limit, so I bought the room back by cutting rendering constraints that do nothing: the column no longer has to stand in the right part of the sheet, and repeated boilerplate was compressed. No disclosed geometry, relationship, or numeral target was traded away to make room.

I changed nothing in the claims, the numeral table, the summary, or the abstract this turn. Every repair was to a figure brief, plus the two sentences of application text that described what a sheet shows and would otherwise have contradicted the repaired brief.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

input.summary: Applied all three findings, which were one defect seen from three sides: the application text still described FIG. 1 as carrying broken-line artwork that the FIG. 1 brief forbids and does not draw. draft/06-drawings.md now reads "FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown in use on a covering element and carrying a handle, the handle, the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being shown schematically." draft/07-detailed-description.md, in the air-extraction mechanism section, now reads "The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings, no particular route being required.", matching the wording already used in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs and adding no route, opening or duct. With the Brief Description no longer promising the chamber on FIG. 1, the numeral-22 expectation is gone, and both FIG. 1 numeral lists correctly stay at 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44. The chamber 22 keeps its numeral-table row, its recitations in the claims and description, and its depiction on FIG. 2 as the broad white space between the legs. No claim, numeral definition, figure brief, or rendered sheet changed. Checked that the rest of the package is intact: claims 1, 10 and 14 still read "placed against" and "brought against", the method paragraph matches, the motor paragraph carries no breadth assertion, the three Background citations are present, and no draft file now contains any reference to a broken line, a dashed line, or hidden artwork.
reasoning: The repair direction was set by the authority order, not by convenience. The FIG. 1 brief states in absolute terms that every line is solid and nothing hidden is drawn, and its geometry list contains no chamber and no communication path. Rewriting the brief to add a hidden chamber outline and a broken communication line would have reintroduced exactly the geometry that caused numerals 20 and 22 to be rejected on that sheet, so the text that described artwork the specification cannot produce is what had to give.

The replacement sentence in the Detailed Description deliberately adds no route. The disclosure says only that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, and an earlier corrective message identified a through-base extraction opening or duct as unsupported. Saying that no particular route is depicted or required states the position without inventing a path across the base, and it uses the same formula as the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs so the whole set now speaks with one voice.

Numeral 22 needed no action once the Brief Description stopped promising it on FIG. 1. It keeps its single definition in draft/numerals.md, remains recited in claims 1, 10 and 14 and throughout the description, and is depicted and labelled on FIG. 2, so the figure-plan rule against dropping a disclosed part is satisfied by redistribution rather than deletion.

Two of these sentences had been corrected in an earlier turn and were back in their original form in the workspace, so I reapplied them rather than assuming the work stood. I then verified the rest of the earlier repairs individually instead of trusting them: the against-wording in all three independent claims and in the method paragraph, the removal of the motor breadth assertion, the handle sentence, and the three Background citations are all present, and no draft file mentions broken, dashed, or hidden line work anywhere.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings, no particular route being required.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
44	
45	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
46	
47	The vibration transmission path
48	
49	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
50	
51	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
52	
53	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
54	
55	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
56	
57	Handles
58	
59	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
60	
61	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
62	
63	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
64	
65	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
66	
67	Method of use
68	
69	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
70

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings, no particular route being required.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38.
