In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings, no particular route being required.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every line is solid, and the sheet contains only the parts listed. No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; apart from the view legend and the sheet number, the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines. The covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile as in FIG. 1, fills the lower part of the sheet and is otherwise plain. - The vibration device 10 is the machine standing on the covering element 36, drawn as on FIG. 1: a base carrying two separate simple housings, the base being shown schematically as a slab and the housings being shown schematically. import re, glob, os

os.chdir(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))
files = sorted(glob.glob('draft/*.md')) + sorted(glob.glob('figures/*.md'))
bad = ['TODO', 'TBD', 'XXX', 'placeholder', 'draftsperson', 'drafter', 'illustrator',
       'reviewer', 'attorney', 'confirm', 'Note:', 'note:', '?', '—', '[', ']']
for f in files:
    t = open(f).read()
    for i, l in enumerate(t.split('\n'), 1):
        for b in bad:
            if b in l:
                print('MARK', f, i, repr(b), l[:100])

print('--- brief lengths')
for f in sorted(glob.glob('figures/*.md')):
    print(len(open(f).read()), f)

print('--- numeral table')
tbl = re.findall(r'^\| (\d+) \| (.+?) \|', open('draft/numerals.md').read(), re.M)
print(tbl)
keys = [k for k, _ in tbl]
print('dupe numerals:', len(keys) != len(set(keys)))
names = [v for _, v in tbl]
print('dupe names:', len(names) != len(set(names)))

print('--- numerals used per file')
for f in files:
    if f.endswith('numerals.md'):
        continue
    used = sorted(set(re.findall(r'\b(\d{2})\b', open(f).read())), key=int)
    print(f, used, 'NOT IN TABLE:', [u for u in used if u not in keys])

1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions whose ends contact the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions whose ends contact the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. 1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12

content.content:
1	A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force being required from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

content.text:
All three review findings are fixed; nothing else in the draft was touched.

**What changed**

1. `draft/07-detailed-description.md:23` — removed the trailing clause "no particular route being required". That clause was an affirmative technical assertion (the fluid-communication route may be anything at all) that the disclosure never makes; it only says fluid communication exists. The sentence now records only the drawing omission: "The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings." The supported statement earlier in the paragraph is untouched, so the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs that say the route "is not depicted in this view" remain consistent with the text.

2. `figures/FIG-5-...md` — numeral 10 now lands on the continuous outer silhouette, as on FIG. 1, instead of on the exposed top face of the base, which FIG. 1 reserves for numeral 12. The two sheets draw the same machine, so a reader carrying FIG. 1's convention across can no longer read the FIG. 5 leader as pointing at the base.

3. `figures/FIG-5-...md` — the pulling element's meeting place with the machine is now marked as a depiction convention in both the opening paragraph and the bullet ("shown schematically, no particular attachment location or attachment formation being shown"). The line still runs away to the left and leaves the sheet at the left edge, because the sheet needs a path and the last bullet places numeral 36 on the exposed tile to the right, away from the line; nothing about attachment was added to `draft/06-drawings.md` or any other section.

**Verified after the edits:** the numeral table's 16 entries are one-to-one with the text, no numeral appears on a sheet that its file does not list, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, every brief is well under 2800 characters, and no note, placeholder, question, human-directed instruction or em dash appears anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`. The only bracketed text in the application is the two `[REF:...]` citations in the Background, both keys drawn from `prior_art/INDEX.md`.

I left one thing alone deliberately: the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs name "the air-extraction mechanism" and "the chamber" without numerals, only to say the route between them is not drawn. Nothing is described as visible there, the Brief Description of the Drawings uses the same wording, and the prior review examined all five briefs and endorsed their treatment of omissions, so rewording it would have desynchronized good text for no gain.

input.summary: Fixed all three findings from the previous review with minimal, targeted edits: deleted the unsupported "no particular route being required" clause from the detailed description, moved FIG. 5's numeral 10 onto the outer silhouette so it no longer collides with FIG. 1's numeral 12 on the same drawn surface, and marked the pulling element's meeting place with the machine as a depiction convention inside the FIG. 5 brief only. No claim, numeral definition, or other section was changed.
reasoning: The critical finding was correct and I applied it as stated. 'No particular route being required' is not a statement about the drawing, it is a statement about the invention: it asserts the arrangement is indifferent to how the air-extraction mechanism reaches the chamber. The disclosure says only that fluid communication exists, and the one corrective USER message that mentions ducts and through-base openings names them for deletion, which is not affirmative support. The cure was silence about the route, not a broader assertion, so the sentence now records only that the route is not depicted. The earlier supported sentence (mechanism coupled to the first side, withdrawing air from the chamber) carries the disclosure content and was left intact.

The FIG. 5 / FIG. 1 numeral collision was a real brief-level defect independent of pixels. Both sheets draw the same machine; FIG. 1 puts 10 on the silhouette and reserves the exposed top face of the base for 12, while FIG. 5 was pointing 10 at that same exposed top face. Since the detailed description opens by saying the same numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings, adopting FIG. 1's silhouette convention on FIG. 5 was the fix that preserved both sheets rather than re-cutting the geometry.

On the pulling-element attachment, I agree it carries technical substance (line of action of the pulling force) and is not disclosed: the inventor says only that a rope, wire or cable is connected to the device. But the drawing has to show the line meeting the machine somewhere, so I marked the meeting place schematic in the brief rather than deleting it, and added nothing about attachment to the Brief Description or any application section. I kept the explicit leftward run and left-edge exit for the line itself, because that is the path of a drawn element rather than an attachment location, and because the covering element 36 endpoint in the last bullet is defined as the tile surface on the side away from the pulling element and would become ambiguous without a run direction.

I did not touch the claims. Claim 1 already rests on the combination that carries it clear of the art: a rigid low-friction perimeter member whose end face is the bearing face, a clearance along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric, foam or resilient member interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Each limitation appears verbatim in the detailed description.

I left the Background alone rather than adding the two uncited references. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated-suction-plate lifting system and US-4934475-A uses vibration to intermittently reduce its own holding force so the body walks along a wall, which is the inverse of delivering vibration into the workpiece while the hold is continuously maintained. Both are distinguishable, but the request and the review asked for targeted repairs, and rewriting the Background to discuss them would have destroyed reviewed text for no gate benefit.

I also declined to change the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs, where 'air-extraction mechanism' and 'chamber' are named without numerals purely to say the route between them is not drawn. structured_output.summary: Fixed all three findings from the previous review with minimal, targeted edits: deleted the unsupported "no particular route being required" clause from the detailed description, moved FIG. 5's numeral 10 onto the outer silhouette so it no longer collides with FIG. 1's numeral 12 on the same drawn surface, and marked the pulling element's meeting place with the machine as a depiction convention inside the FIG. 5 brief only. No claim, numeral definition, or other section was changed.
reasoning: The critical finding was correct and I applied it as stated. 'No particular route being required' is not a statement about the drawing, it is a statement about the invention: it asserts the arrangement is indifferent to how the air-extraction mechanism reaches the chamber. The disclosure says only that fluid communication exists, and the one corrective USER message that mentions ducts and through-base openings names them for deletion, which is not affirmative support. The cure was silence about the route, not a broader assertion, so the sentence now records only that the route is not depicted. The earlier supported sentence (mechanism coupled to the first side, withdrawing air from the chamber) carries the disclosure content and was left intact.

The FIG. 5 / FIG. 1 numeral collision was a real brief-level defect independent of pixels. Both sheets draw the same machine; FIG. 1 puts 10 on the silhouette and reserves the exposed top face of the base for 12, while FIG. 5 was pointing 10 at that same exposed top face. Since the detailed description opens by saying the same numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings, adopting FIG. 1's silhouette convention on FIG. 5 was the fix that preserved both sheets rather than re-cutting the geometry.

On the pulling-element attachment, I agree it carries technical substance (line of action of the pulling force) and is not disclosed: the inventor says only that a rope, wire or cable is connected to the device. But the drawing has to show the line meeting the machine somewhere, so I marked the meeting place schematic in the brief rather than deleting it, and added nothing about attachment to the Brief Description or any application section. I kept the explicit leftward run and left-edge exit for the line itself, because that is the path of a drawn element rather than an attachment location, and because the covering element 36 endpoint in the last bullet is defined as the tile surface on the side away from the pulling element and would become ambiguous without a run direction.

I did not touch the claims. Claim 1 already rests on the combination that carries it clear of the art: a rigid low-friction perimeter member whose end face is the bearing face, a clearance along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric, foam or resilient member interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Each limitation appears verbatim in the detailed description.

I left the Background alone rather than adding the two uncited references. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated-suction-plate lifting system and US-4934475-A uses vibration to intermittently reduce its own holding force so the body walks along a wall, which is the inverse of delivering vibration into the workpiece while the hold is continuously maintained. Both are distinguishable, but the request and the review asked for targeted repairs, and rewriting the Background to discuss them would have destroyed reviewed text for no gate benefit.

I also declined to change the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs, where 'air-extraction mechanism' and 'chamber' are named without numerals purely to say the route between them is not drawn. Nothing is described as visible, the Brief Description of the Drawings uses matching language, and the prior review affirmatively found the briefs and the description agreed on what each sheet omits. Editing them would desynchronize three files to silence a check that did not fire.

FIG. 5's brief is now under the limit; nothing else changed.

**What I cut, and why each was safe**

The brief was 21 characters over the 2800 limit after last turn's two required corrections were added to it. I removed only invented rendering constraints, keeping every disclosure-grounded relationship, every numeral, and both prior fixes intact:

- `figures/FIG-5-...md:7` — dropped "and is otherwise plain" from the covering element sentence. It was redundant: the same sentence already calls it "one large plain tile".
- `figures/FIG-5-...md:11` — dropped "and the only curving element on the sheet" from the flexible pulling element 46 bullet. The bullet already identifies it as "the one slack flexible line on the sheet, drawn as a single curved path of even thickness", which is the description the cord guidance calls for; the extra clause was a stroke-counting constraint doing no work.
- `figures/FIG-5-...md:10` — "outward-facing front surface" became "front surface" in the perimeter member 24 bullet, matching the wording of that bullet's own endpoint sentence ("well inside that visible front surface").

The file went from 2930 bytes to 2850. The gate measured 2821 against a 2930-byte file, so it counts the body at 109 characters below file size; the same body now measures about 2741, leaving roughly 59 characters of margin. FIG. 1 (2792 bytes) and FIG. 4 (2798 bytes) sit further under once their own title and trailing numeral list are discounted, and neither was flagged.

**Preserved from last turn:** numeral 10 still lands on the continuous outer silhouette clear of the flexible pulling element 46, so it does not collide with FIG. 1's numeral 12 on the base's top face; the meeting place of the pulling element with the machine is still marked "shown schematically, no particular attachment location or attachment formation being shown" in both the opening paragraph and the bullet; the line still runs left and exits the left edge, keeping the covering element 36 endpoint on the opposite side unambiguous. The numeral list for the sheet is unchanged at 10, 24, 36, 46, so the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description and the other four briefs stay synchronized. No file in `draft/` needed an edit this turn.

input.summary: Brought the FIG. 5 figure brief under the 2800-character limit by removing three redundant rendering constraints, with no change to the patent text, claims, numeral table, disclosed geometry, or the two corrections made in the previous turn. The brief dropped from 2930 to 2850 bytes on disk, which is about 2741 by the gate's own count, leaving roughly 59 characters of margin.
reasoning: The single failing check was a length overrun of 21 characters on FIG. 5, caused by the two corrections the previous review required me to add to that brief (the schematic attachment qualifier in the opening paragraph and again in the pulling-element bullet). Since both of those are substantive source-fidelity fixes, the characters had to come out of the invented rendering constraints instead.

I calibrated against the gate's own arithmetic rather than guessing: the gate reported 2821 for a file that was 2930 bytes, so it discounts 109 characters of title and trailing numeral list. Cutting 80 bytes of body puts the measured value near 2741, which is real margin rather than a one-character pass that the next edit would break.
Cut one: 'and is otherwise plain' was redundant with 'one large plain tile' in the same sentence, so removing it loses no instruction to the renderer.

Cut two: 'and the only curving element on the sheet' was a stroke-counting constraint on the cord, exactly the kind of definition the drawing guidance says not to use. The bullet already identifies the pulling element as the one slack flexible line on the sheet drawn as a single curved path, which is the required description, so the clause was doing no work.

Cut three: 'outward-facing front surface' became 'front surface', which also makes the bullet self-consistent, since its endpoint sentence already refers to 'that visible front surface'. This is a wording tightening, not a geometry change.

I deliberately did not touch the constraints that carry technical or endpoint meaning: the schematic attachment qualifier in both places, the leftward run and left-edge exit (which the covering element 36 endpoint on the opposite side depends on), 'without doubling back or crossing itself', the silhouette target for numeral 10, and the statement that the perimeter member is the only part touching the covering element. Trimming any of those would have traded a length failure for a source-fidelity or endpoint failure.

No file in draft/ was edited. The sheet's numeral membership is unchanged at 10, 24, 36 and 46, so the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description and the other four briefs remain synchronized without any compensating change.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the edits were confined to rendering constraints in one figure brief and touched no claim, no description text and no citation. Claim 1 still rests on the combination that carries it clear of the references: against DE-202021002652-U1, whose tile-setting vibrator grips through suction cups each formed by a rubber-elastic apron, claim 1 recites a rigid low-friction perimeter member in a transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed. Against US-11408462-B2, whose decompressed space is bounded by elastic partitions stiffened by a frame member so they are not drawn inward, claim 1 recites the deliberate clearance along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air enters continuously while the extraction rate holds the chamber below atmospheric. Against US-10001245-B2, which holds by vacuum and then switches its pneumatic generator to blower mode to ride an air cushion while it moves, claim 1 recites that the bearing face is slidable while the pressure differential is maintained, so holding and sliding are simultaneous rather than alternative modes. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction plate for lifting sheet material, and US-4934475-A uses its vibration generator to periodically reduce its own holding force so the body walks along a wall, which is the inverse of delivering vibration into the workpiece under a continuously maintained hold; neither supplies the continuous-ingress-plus-excess-extraction relationship. Citations remain confined to the Background and use only keys from prior_art/INDEX.md.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The route by which the air-extraction mechanism 20 communicates with the chamber 22 is not depicted in the drawings.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24 shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
