input.summary: Applied all three residual source-fidelity fixes: removed the two sentences of drafting commentary announcing what the drawings omit (one in the detailed description, one in the Brief Description of FIG. 2), softened the handle paragraph back to the disclosure's "primarily to guide rather than to press", and made FIG. 4 refer to the same perimeter member 24 as FIG. 2 in the description and the FIG. 4 brief. Claims, numeral table and Summary untouched.
reasoning: The omission commentary had to come out of the filing text rather than be cured by drawing the route. Claims 1, 10 and 14 all positively recite the air-extraction mechanism as in fluid communication with the chamber, so announcing in the text that the route is not drawn advertised the 37 CFR 1.83(a) exposure instead of just leaving it. Adding a duct or through-base opening would have been the wrong cure: the disclosure says only that fluid communication exists, and a duct was expressly named as unsupported in the corrective USER message. Deleting the sentences leaves the supported statement (mechanism coupled to the first side, withdrawing air from the chamber) carrying the disclosure content.

I kept the parallel negative instructions inside the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs. Those are renderer guidance about what not to draw, they live in the figure specifications rather than in filing text, and the review identified them as legitimate. Removing them would have invited the image model to invent a route, which is the failure mode the authority order exists to prevent.

The handle wording was an overstatement I had to walk back to the source. The disclosure says the handles are used primarily for guiding rather than pressing, which leaves pressing possible but not the handle's purpose; the description had hardened that into an absolute 'is not used to press'. Because the overstatement was confined to the description and claim 8 recites only 'a handle arranged to guide', the conform-to-source edit carries no claim consequence, so I left claim 8 and the Summary alone.

The FIG. 4 hedge was a genuine antecedent problem, not a stylistic one: 'a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2' reads as a possibly different member wearing the same numeral, which breaks the rule that one numeral denotes one part throughout. The hedge was never needed, because 'along at least part of the perimeter member' already explains how FIG. 4 (taken where the clearance is present) sits with FIG. 2 (legs resting on the covering element at that view's scale). I made the same change in the FIG. 4 brief so the description, the brief and the Brief Description entry now agree, and left the depicted clearance untouched.

I changed no geometry and regenerated no relationship to suit a rendering. The FIG. 4 edit shortened that brief by 18 characters, which also widened its margin under the length gate that failed two turns ago; FIG. 5 remains at 2850 bytes, about 2741 by the gate's own count.

Against US-11408462-B2, whose decompressed space is bounded by elastic partitions stiffened by a frame member so they are not drawn inward, claim 1 recites the deliberate clearance along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air enters continuously while the extraction rate keeps the chamber below atmospheric. Against US-10001245-B2, which holds by vacuum and then switches its pneumatic generator to blower mode to ride an air cushion while it moves, claim 1 recites a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained, making holding and sliding simultaneous rather than alternative modes. Citations remain confined to the Background and use only keys from prior_art/INDEX.md.

Both findings are fixed in the figure briefs; no application text, claim, numeral or embodiment changed.

**1. FIG. 4 no longer drives line work onto the sheet edges** (`figures/FIG-4-...md`)

- The column now runs "unbroken from the upper limit of the drawing area, where the column is broken off", preserving the fragmentary character of the view while keeping the break inside the drawing area.
- The three layer bands each span "the full width of the drawing area", and the exposed face 38 line runs "unbroken across the drawing area".
- Added the margin sentence used by the other briefs: "The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet."
- For consistency I also changed "across the lower part of the sheet" to "across the lower part of the drawing area" in the same paragraph, so nothing in the brief still points the artwork at a sheet edge.

To absorb the added wording I removed one redundant phrase, ", the lowest line of that column", from the bearing face 26 bullet; the line is already identified as "the single horizontal line closing the bottom of the column", and its endpoint sentence is unchanged. FIG. 4 is 2858 bytes on disk, about 2734 by the gate's own count, comfortably under the 2800 limit.

**2. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 no longer assert a solid, featureless base** (`figures/FIG-2-...md`, `figures/FIG-3-...md`)

- FIG. 2 now reads: "The base 12 is hatched where the section passes through it. The section plane is taken clear of the route by which the air-extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber, so that route is not depicted in this view." The omission is now a consequence of where the section is taken rather than a positive statement that the base is unbroken, which no longer contradicts the fluid communication recited in claims 1, 10 and 14 and described in the detailed description.
- FIG. 3 now reads "The interior of the innermost rectangle is left plain; the route by which the air-extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber is not depicted in this view."
- I also changed "spanning the full width" to "spanning the full width of the drawing area" in the FIG. 2 covering element 36 bullet, so that brief's margin convention is unambiguous throughout.

No duct, opening or other route structure was added anywhere, since the disclosure supplies none.

**Synchronization:** numeral membership per sheet is unchanged (FIG. 2: 12, 14, 22, 24, 36; FIG. 3: 16, 24; FIG. 4: 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42), so the 16-entry numeral table, the five Brief Description entries, the detailed description and the claims all remain in step, and every brief is under the length limit at 2792, 2363, 2241, 2858 and 2850 bytes. No note, placeholder, question or instruction to a person appears in `draft/` or `figures/`.

reasoning: The FIG. 4 edge problem was a drawing-space defect with no bearing on the invention, so I fixed it purely as a rendering instruction: the column now breaks at the upper limit of the drawing area rather than at the sheet edge, which keeps the view fragmentary (the break is what makes it a fragmentary section) while leaving a margin. The bands and the exposed face line were retargeted from the sheet to the drawing area for the same reason, and I added the identical margin sentence that FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 already carry so the whole set now states one convention.

I also changed 'across the lower part of the sheet' to 'across the lower part of the drawing area' in that same paragraph. The reviewer did not list it, but leaving one sheet-referenced placement instruction beside four drawing-area ones would have left the brief internally ambiguous about which boundary governs, which is the condition the finding is about.

Adding the margin wording pushed FIG. 4 toward the 2800 limit that failed two turns ago, so I paid for it by deleting ', the lowest line of that column' from the bearing face 26 bullet. That phrase was redundant with 'the single horizontal line closing the bottom of the column' in the same sentence, and the endpoint instruction that distinguishes the line from the hatching above and the space below is untouched. FIG. 4 now measures about 2734 by the gate's count.

The FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 defect was the more consequential one, because it was a drawing positively contradicting a claim limitation. Claims 1, 10 and 14 all recite the air-extraction mechanism as in fluid communication with the chamber, and 'hatched throughout' plus 'plain white paper' drew a base with no communication at all. The cure had to preserve the source-fidelity behaviour that produced those words in the first place: the disclosure gives no route, and a through-base duct was expressly identified as unsupported, so I could not draw one. Recasting the omission as a consequence of where the section plane and the view are taken removes the contradiction without adding any structure.

I made the parallel 'spanning the full width' to 'full width of the drawing area' change in the FIG. 2 covering element bullet, since FIG. 2 states the margin convention and that bullet was the one place in it still measured against the sheet.

The margin convention is now uniform across all five briefs; no application text changed.

**FIG. 5** (`figures/FIG-5-...md`)
- The flexible pulling element 46 is now "broken off short of the left-hand limit of the drawing area in one unbroken path, without doubling back or crossing itself" instead of leaving the sheet at its left edge. It still meets the machine, runs away to the left over the covering element 36 and sags gently, so it remains the rope, wire or cable connected to the device, with no length, attachment location or attachment formation asserted.
- The covering element 36 now "fills the lower part of the drawing area".
- Added "The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet." at the end of the geometry section.

**FIG. 1** (`figures/FIG-1-...md`)
- The covering element 36 now "fills the lower part of the drawing area", and the same margin sentence was added at the end of the geometry section.

**Length management.** Adding the margin wording would have pushed FIG. 5 over the 2800 limit, so I removed three invented rendering constraints from that brief to pay for it: the duplicated "meets the outer silhouette of the machine and" in the opening paragraph (the bullet for 46 states the same thing and keeps the schematic-meeting-place qualifier, which also still appears in the opening paragraph); "of even thickness" on the cord, leaving it described as a single curved path; and "but from further off" in the View line. I also condensed the schematic wording in the vibration device 10 bullet without changing what it depicts. FIG. 5 is 2855 bytes on disk, about 2746 by the gate's count; FIG. 1 is 2865, about 2738; FIG. 4 is 2858, about 2734. All five are under the limit.

**Synchronization:** no file in `draft/` was touched, and numeral membership per sheet is unchanged (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44; FIG. 5: 10, 24, 36, 46), so the 16-entry numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description and the claims all remain in step. input.summary: Fixed the one verified defect: FIG. 5 no longer directs the flexible pulling element off the sheet edge, and both FIG. 5 and FIG. 1 now measure the tile against the drawing area and carry the same margin sentence as FIGS. 2, 3 and 4. To keep FIG. 5 under the 2800-character limit I removed three invented rendering constraints from that brief. No claim, description, numeral definition or embodiment was touched.
reasoning: The finding was a drawing-space contradiction between briefs, so the whole fix stays in the briefs. Breaking the cord short of the left-hand limit of the drawing area preserves everything the disclosure supports about it: it is still a flexible line connected to the device, running away over the covering element, with no length, attachment location or attachment formation asserted. A broken-off line is the ordinary way to show an element continuing beyond the view, so nothing about the embodiment changes.

Applying the fix as written would have pushed FIG. 5 from about 2741 to about 2843 by the gate's count, re-triggering the length failure from an earlier turn. I paid for the added margin wording out of invented rendering constraints rather than out of anything grounded: the opening paragraph's 'meets the outer silhouette of the machine and' duplicated the bullet for 46; 'of even thickness' was surplus once the cord is described as a single curved path, which is what the cord guidance asks for; and 'but from further off' was an arbitrary viewpoint constraint.

I kept the schematic-meeting-place qualifier in both the opening paragraph and the bullet even though it costs characters. That wording is what a previous review required to stop the brief fixing an undisclosed attachment location, so trimming it to save space would have traded a formal defect for a source-fidelity one.

In the vibration device 10 bullet I condensed 'the base being shown schematically as a slab and the housings being shown schematically' to 'the base and the housings all being shown schematically, the base as a slab'. Same depiction, same schematic labelling of both conventions, fewer characters.

The numeral endpoint for 46 still reads 'clear of the edges of the sheet'. That is a label-placement constraint keeping the numeral inside the margin, not an instruction to draw line work to the edge, so it agrees with the new margin sentence rather than contradicting it.

FIG. 1 needed the same two changes even though only FIG. 5 was named in the check line, because the reviewer identified the tile-against-sheet measurement in both briefs and a single set-wide convention is what makes the check unambiguous. Nothing in draft/ required an edit, and no sheet's numeral membership moved, so the table, Brief Description, description and claims stayed synchronized on their own.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto the covering element 36. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every line on the sheet is a solid line; no broken, dashed or dotted line appears anywhere, and nothing hidden behind a body is drawn. No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; apart from the view legend and the sheet number, the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines. The view legend reads FIG. 1 and is placed below the drawing, clear of all line work and leaders.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile, fills the lower part of the drawing area. A machine stands on it. Two separate housings are carried on the top face of the base 12, and a grip is carried on the machine; the housings, the grip and the base 12 are all shown schematically, the base 12 as a slab.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that silhouette.
- The base 12 is the slab that carries the two housings; its top face remains visible where no housing stands on it. Identified well inside that visible part of the top face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the loop or skirt, shown schematically as a shallow band, standing under the base 12 and running round its underside at its edge, so the base 12 stands clear of the covering element 36; its front surface is visible below the base 12, and it is the only part of the vibration device 10 touching the covering element 36. Identified well inside that front surface, clear of the corners where the band turns.
- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand of the two housings on the top face of the base 12, shown schematically as a simple closed housing. Its front face is a plain closed surface that no other line crosses. Identified well inside that front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand of the two housings on the top face of the base 12, shown schematically as a separate simple closed housing. Its front face is a plain closed surface that no other line crosses. Identified well inside that front face.
- The handle 44 is shown schematically as a simple grip carried on the machine above the base 12 and clear of the two housings, drawn as one closed outline that encloses a visible open area of its own; no particular handle form is shown. Identified well inside that enclosed open area.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside its exposed upper surface, clear of the machine.

The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every line is solid, and the sheet contains only the parts listed. **Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile as in FIG. 1, fills the lower part of the drawing area. A machine stands on it, and the surface of the covering element 36 is exposed around the machine. The flexible pulling element 46 runs away to the left over the covering element 36; the place at which it meets the machine is shown schematically, no particular attachment location or attachment formation being shown.

- The vibration device 10 is the machine standing on the covering element 36, drawn as on FIG. 1: a base carrying two separate simple housings, the base and the housings all being shown schematically, the base as a slab. Identified well inside that visible front surface, clear of the corners where the band turns.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is the one slack flexible line on the sheet, drawn as a single curved path. It meets the outer silhouette of the vibration device 10, that meeting place being shown schematically, then runs away to the left over the covering element 36, sagging gently, and is broken off short of the left-hand limit of the drawing area in one unbroken path, without doubling back or crossing itself. Identified on that curved line at a place where it runs over the covering element 36, clear of the vibration device 10 and clear of the edges of the sheet.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the vibration device 10 stands. Identified well inside the exposed surface of that tile on the right of the machine, on the side away from the flexible pulling element 46, clear of the machine.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the base, with the covering element removed. Outline line work only: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed or double line, every outline one thin line. No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; apart from the view legend and the sheet number, the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines. The view legend reads FIG. 3 and is placed below the drawing, clear of all line work and leaders.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The closed loop is shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline, this being a depiction convention for this sheet only. The whole sheet contains exactly two rectangular outlines, one nested inside the other, and no other line of any kind. The outermost rectangle is the outer edge of the perimeter member 24; because this view looks straight at the underside of the base, the edge of the base is that same single line, and no separate outline is drawn for the base. The innermost rectangle is the inner edge of the perimeter member 24. Each of the two rectangles is one closed thin line, and no third rectangle, no frame and no border appears on the sheet.

Those two outlines enclose two surfaces: the band between them, and the plain field inside the innermost rectangle.

The two rectangles are spaced apart on all four sides, so that the band between them is a continuous visible surface running all the way round.

The interior of the innermost rectangle is left plain; the route by which the air-extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber is not depicted in this view.

The drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet.

- The perimeter member 24 is the band between the two rectangles, the closed loop seen end on. Identified well inside that band, clear of the corners where the band turns.
- The second side 16 is the underside face of the base, which this view looks straight at, and it shows within the perimeter member 24 as the field inside the innermost rectangle. Identified well inside that field, clear of the band.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24

content.text:
The gate reported a crash (`'NoneType' object is not iterable`) with no content finding attached, so I removed the one structural irregularity in the workspace and made the figure-brief set uniform.

**What was irregular.** In the previous turn I appended the margin sentence to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 *after* their numeral bullet lists, so those two files had a prose paragraph sitting between the bullets and the `**Numerals appearing on this figure:**` line. FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 all place that sentence *before* the bullets, leaving the bullet list as the last block. That difference was introduced in exactly the turn preceding this failure and is the kind of shape variance a brief parser is sensitive to.

**Changes** (all in `figures/`, byte-for-byte relocations except one word-level edit):
- `FIG-1-...md` — "The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet." moved from after the bullet list to its own paragraph before it.
- `FIG-5-...md` — same relocation.
- `FIG-3-...md` — "The drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet." became "The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet.", so all five briefs now state the margin convention in identical words.

**Verified after the edits.** Every brief now runs View block, `**Geometry to be drawn**`, prose paragraphs ending with the margin sentence, numeral bullets, `**Numerals appearing on this figure:**`, `## Numerals shown on this figure` — confirmed by marker line numbers in all five files. Lengths are 2865, 2363, 2254, 2858 and 2855 bytes, all under the limit once the gate's title-and-list discount is applied. All nine `draft/` sections and `numerals.md` are non-empty and were not touched this turn; numeral membership per sheet is unchanged (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44; FIG. 2: 12, 14, 22, 24, 36; FIG. 3: 16, 24; FIG. 4: 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42; FIG. 5: 10, 24, 36, 46), so the numeral table, Brief Description of the Drawings, detailed description and claims remain synchronized. No note, placeholder, question or instruction to a person appears anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`.

I could not inspect the gate's own source (`src/` is outside the permitted path), so this fix targets the workspace-side condition I can control and verify.

I made the relocation byte-neutral: the sentence is the same text, just moved, so FIG. 1 stays at 2865 and FIG. 5 at 2855 bytes, both under the length gate that failed two turns ago. I did not take the opportunity to rewrite anything else in those briefs.

I also brought FIG. 3's variant wording ('The drawing stands clear...') into line with the other four ('The whole of the drawing stands clear...'). One sentence in one form across the set removes the last piece of variance in how the margin convention is expressed, at a cost of 13 bytes in the shortest brief.

None of this touched the invention: the margin convention is a drawing-space instruction, the relocation changes no geometry, no relationship, no endpoint and no numeral membership, and draft/01-09 and numerals.md were not opened for editing.

Claim 1 still rests on the combination that carries it clear of the references: against DE-202021002652-U1, whose tile-setting vibrator grips through suction cups each formed by a rubber-elastic apron, claim 1 recites a rigid low-friction perimeter member in a transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed. Against US-11408462-B2, whose decompressed space is bounded by elastic partitions stiffened by a frame member so they are not drawn inward, claim 1 recites the deliberate clearance along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air enters continuously while the extraction rate keeps the chamber below atmospheric. Against US-10001245-B2, which holds by vacuum and then switches its pneumatic generator to blower mode to ride an air cushion while it moves, claim 1 recites a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained, so holding and sliding are simultaneous rather than alternative modes. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction plate for lifting sheet material, and US-4934475-A uses its vibration generator to periodically reduce its own holding force so the body walks along a wall, the inverse of delivering vibration into the workpiece under a continuously maintained hold. Citations remain confined to the Background and use only keys from prior_art/INDEX.md.
